Leveraging Propargyl Sulfides as Radical Trappers for the
Synthesis of Sulfonyl Allenes
Qi Zhang
+
,
[a]
Zhongtian Wu
+
,
[a]
Yifan Sun
+
,
[a]
Xiancheng Qiu,
[a]
Huiying Liu,
[a]
Xinxin Wu,*
[a]
and Chen Zhu*
[a, b]
This work showcases a novel visible-light mediated allenylation
protocol employing propargyl sulfides as a pioneering radical
trapping methodology. A diverse array of substituted sulfonyl
allenes were successfully synthesized under mild conditions
with commendable levels of chemo- and regio-selectivity.
Mechanistically, this process entails the formation of sulfonyl
radicals, their subsequent addition to alkynes, the subsequent
elimination of S-centered radicals, and Cl-atom abstraction,
thereby facilitating the propagation of this radical chain
reaction.
Introduction
Allenes constitute a significant category of organic compounds
characterized by distinctive twisted orthogonal π-systems.
[1]
They serve as pivotal structural units in numerous natural
products and pharmaceuticals, showcasing their prominence in
both medicinal chemistry and natural product synthesis. Addi-
tionally, they emerge as highly versatile synthons in contempo-
rary organic synthesis methodologies, facilitating the construc-
tion of diverse molecular architectures and enabling efficient
design strategies for bioactive molecules. A plethora of method-
ologies for the synthesis of allenes have been extensively
documented in the literature. In pursuit of advancing increas-
ingly reliable methodologies, there has been a rapid surge in
the utilization of radical species for the synthesis of allenes. This
radical approach has recently received significant attention and
its potential has been convincingly demonstrated.
[2]
These
include radical 1,4-addition to 1,3-enynes,
[3]
radical synthesis of
allenes from propargylic compounds,
[4]
radical allene C(sp
2
)-H
functionalization,
[5]
and various other efficient synthetic
routes.
[6]
As an important complement to previous studies, the
radical-mediated conversion of propargylic compounds into
allenes has emerged as a versatile synthetic route in recent
years (Scheme 1A). For instance, Cárdenas and coworkers
observed that rather than yielding propargylic compounds,
nickel-catalyzed the cross-coupling reaction between alkylzinc
halides and propargyl bromides, provides a pathway to access
allenes (Scheme 1A, top).
[4a]
In 2020, Xu and Lan et al. reported a photocatalytic radical
synthesis of functionalized allenes under visible-light irradiation
(Scheme 1A, middle).
[4b]
This method utilizes readily accessible
terminal alkynyl aziridines. In 2021, the Liang group disclosed a
photoredox/nickel dual-catalyzed alkylation approach employ-
ing propargylic carbonates and alkyl 1,4-dihydropyridine deriv-
atives (1,4-DHPs) serving as alkyl radical precursors (Scheme 1A,
bottom).
[4c]
Liu et al. pioneered a novel approach for the direct
synthesis of chiral allenes through enantioselective copper-
catalyzed cyanation of propargylic C � H bonds.
[4d]
Studer and
colleagues reported a example of radical allylation employing a
homoallylic alcohol, albeit yielding modestly.
[7]
In 2021, Zhu and
coworkers disclosed the radical chain isomerization of N-

radicals to ynamides.
[8]
As a result, radical synthesis of allenes
from propargylic compounds via C � C bond formation has been
extensively explored. However, to the best of our knowledge,
radical synthesis of allenes from propargylic compounds via C-
heteroatom bond formation has been scarcely documented.
Motivated by our interest in radical-mediated allene
synthesis,
[9]
we postulated that the addition of a heteroatom-
centered radical to propargylic compounds could lead to the
formation of corresponding allenes via C-heteroatom bond
formation under mild conditions. To achieve this transforma-
tion, several challenging issues should be addressed: (1)
Considering the high reactivity of the allene products, strategies
need to be devised to prevent further transformations of the
products.
[10]
(2) When employing internal alkynes, methods for
controlling site-selectivity during the radical addition process
are crucial. (3) Mechanistically, the generation of thiyl radicals
would be generated. Strategies should be developed to prevent
their addition to the alkyne substrate or the allene product.
Herein, we present experimental evidence supporting this
hypothesis (Scheme 1B). Employing propargylic sulfides as
substrates, the reaction proceeds through the addition of a
sulfonyl radical to the alkyne followed by the elimination of an
S-centered radical. Notably, this transformation operates under
mild visible-light-mediated photocatalytic conditions and af-
fords valuable sulfonyl allenes.
Results and Discussion
At the outset, propargylic sulfide (1 a) was selected as the
model substrate to undergo reaction with tosyl chloride (2 a) as
the precursor of tosyl radical under photocatalytic conditions.
The reaction furnished the desired allene product (3 a) utilizing
fac-Ir(ppy)
3
as the photocatalyst. Several parameters, such as
solvent, and additive, were systematically examined to optimize
the reaction conditions (Table 1). Taking into account that H
2
O
may aid in the dissolution of the inorganic base, we firstly
conducted optimization of mixed solvents (entries 1–6). It was
observed that the utilization of CHCl
3
/H
2
O resulted in a higher
yield (39 %, entry 2). A range of bases, such as KHCO
3
, 4-
Dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP), and Et
3
N, were subsequently
evaluated (entries 7–10), revealing that exclusion of the base
led to an improved yield (entry 10). However, the reaction
performed in the absence of H
2
O resulted in a decreased yield
(entry 11). Intriguingly, reducing the reaction concentration
markedly enhanced the yield (entry 12). The conversion of
substrate (2 a) reached approximately 95 %. A side product,
alkene (SP), was formed with a yield of 30 % via the atom
transfer radical addition (ATRA) process. Furthermore, control
experiments demonstrated the essential roles of the photo-
catalyst and blue light irradiation in the reaction (entries 13–14).
With the optimized conditions established for the synthesis
of sulfonyl allenes, the compatibility of various propargylic
sulfides and sulfonyl chlorides was investigated (Scheme 2).
Common functional groups on the phenyl ring, such as ether
(3 b), benzene (3 f), nitrile (3 g), ketone (3 h), halides (3 i--3 k),
nitro group (3 o), and trifluoromethyl group (3 p), exhibited
compatibility under the reaction conditions. Regardless of the
presence of electron-withdrawing or -donating substituents at
the para-position of the phenyl ring, the reactions proceeded
smoothly to afford synthetically valuable yields (3 a–3 k). Phenyl-
sulfonyl chlorides bearing ortho-, meta- or di-substituents
underwent facile allenylation (3 l--3 r), albeit the ortho-methyl
substituent resulted in a relatively lower yield (3 m). Substituting
the phenyl group with a naphthyl group (3 s), thienyl group
(3 u), or a chromone moiety (3 t) yielded the corresponding
products with slightly reduced yields. It is noteworthy that
reactions with alkyl sulfonyl chlorides efficiently furnished the
desired allenes (3 v--3 x). Internal alkynes bearing with sulfide
could also effectively trap the sulfonyl radical, affording 1,1-
disubstituted allenes (3 y) with excellent chemo- and regio-
selectivity. Additionally, employing secondary aryl sulfides
bearing various alkyl moieties led to the formation of 1,3-
disubstituted allenes (3 z--3 ac) in synthetically useful yields.
The scaled-up synthesis of 3 a utilizing flow chemistry
techniques proceeded smoothly,
[11]
yielding a comparable
result, thus underscoring the practicality of the protocol
(Scheme 3A). To investigate the mechanistic pathway, we
employed high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) for reac-

tion detection, revealing the presence of disulfide (Scheme 3B).
Subsequently, light on/off experiments were performed on the
model reaction, demonstrating that the reaction yield increased
even when light was turned off (Scheme 3C). This observation
suggests that the reaction operates via a radical chain process.
Based on these findings and previous literatures, a plausible
mechanism for this radical-chain process is proposed in
Scheme 4. Initially, the reaction is initiated by single-electron
transfer (SET) between the excited Ir(III)* species and sulfonyl
chloride (2). This results in the formation of the sulfonyl radical
(I), which subsequently adds to alkyne (1) to generate the vinyl
radical (II).
[12]
The subsequent elimination of the thiyl radical (III)
occurs, leading to the formation of product (3). Dimerization of
the thiyl radical (III) yields disulfide (IV). Concurrently, the
generation of the sulfonyl radical is facilitated via Cl-atom
transfer mediated by the thiyl radical (III),
[13]
thus perpetuating
the radical chain process.
Conclusions
We present a novel photocatalytic allenylation protocol utilizing
propargyl sulfides as a new radical trapping agent. The radical-
chain mechanism involves sequential steps including addition
of a sulfonyl radical to the alkyne, elimination of a thiyl radical,
and chloride atom transfer. A diverse array of sulfonyl radicals
readily undergo radical trapping by a range of propargyl
sulfides. This methodology offers an efficient and gentle means
for the synthesis of valuable sulfonyl allenes.
